solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: S takes part of Semiramis in familiar French address

definitions.note: throughout this puzzle the single letter S stands for a sweet, a dessert course

indicators.note: the extracted letters sit inside the French pronoun, so in signals a container

parts.note: tu is the intimate French word for you, used to friends and family

indicators.note: only a portion of the queen's name is used, losing its first three letters

explanation.surface: A note about the Assyrian queen Semiramis being addressed informally in French.
explanation.walkthrough: S standing for a sweet is the puzzle's running device, never explained by a preamble; the Assyrian queen Semiramis is pure surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiramisu is an Italian dessert of coffee-soaked sponge and mascarpone, a classic sweet course.

clue.text: Sort of Celtic crown prince removing odour from plant expert

indicators.note: taking away tells us letters are dropped from the plant specialist

parts.note: a botanist studies plants
BO is body odour

explanation.surface: An odd scene of a Celtic heir being deodorised by a botanist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'removing' strips BO (body odour) from the front of BOTANIST. The Irish deputy prime minister's title, Tánaiste, comes from the same root.
explanation.definitionFit: A tanist was the elected heir apparent of a Celtic chief in old Ireland and Scotland.

clue.text: Of body, list of duties with automatic weapon coming up

indicators.note: in a down clue going upwards means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: a rota lists who does which duty when
a Luger is a German semi-automatic pistol

explanation.surface: Sounds like an anatomy note about bodily duties alongside a gun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming up' turns the whole run ROTALUGER backwards. 'Of' is the prefix of British regulators such as Ofcom and Ofsted, so an 'Of body' is a regulator.
explanation.definitionFit: British watchdog bodies named Of-something (Ofcom, Ofwat, Ofsted) are official regulators of an industry.

clue.text: Kept quiet when bad name included the heartless

indicators.note: one piece is taken within the other, so included signals a container

parts.note: mud is a bad reputation, as in 'his name is mud'

indicators.note: losing its heart means the central letter of the little word goes

explanation.surface: Someone stayed silent when an insult was dropped into the conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad name' is not an anagram signal for NAME: a person whose 'name is mud' has a bad reputation.
explanation.definitionFit: Muted describes sound softened or silenced, the state of being kept quiet.

clue.text: Pleasant but not S

definitions.meaning: ... can mean agreeable or morally wholesome, as in 'not a ... character'
with S standing for sweet, the opposite flavour of a dish is salty or spicy

explanation.walkthrough: S stands for a sweet throughout; a savoury is also the old British after-dinner course served instead of a pudding.
explanation.definitionFit: Savoury means both agreeable in character and salty rather than sweet in taste.

clue.text: See 14
Frank has a problem with those receptive to new ideas

parts.note: frank means candid, open
to mind something is to object to it

explanation.surface: A man called Frank has trouble with people who welcome new thinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like a name but is the adjective meaning candid.
explanation.definitionFit: People with open minds are willing to consider fresh notions.

clue.text: S, possibly first about turn for a boy

indicators.note: moving letters about means they are rearranged

parts.note: a U-turn, so U stands for turn
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: Perhaps a boy turning about at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like a container signal, but it shuffles the fodder; 'turn' gives U via the U-turn.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit salad is a dessert of chopped fresh fruit, one example of a sweet.

clue.text: S for school services' social centre

parts.note: Eton is the famous English public school
the mess is where members of the armed services eat and socialise

explanation.surface: Something served at a school for its forces' canteen.
explanation.walkthrough: ETON is England's best-known boarding school; a MESS is a military dining hall.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton mess is an English dessert of strawberries, cream and broken meringue.

clue.text: Local holding for example? No

indicators.note: one piece holds another, so it surrounds it

parts.note: a local is a native of a place
e.g. is the abbreviation for exempli gratia, for example

explanation.surface: A villager being asked for an example and refusing.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that the definition is a noun stretched from the single reply word.
explanation.definitionFit: A negative is a reply of no, a refusal or denial.

clue.text: Note — ut, possibly — kept going for longer

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A music theory aside about the old sol-fa syllable ut being a note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges NOTE and UT; ut is the old name for the first sol-fa note, now do.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenuto is a musical direction that a note be held for its full value.

clue.text: Party animal?

definitions.meaning: a groom's pre-wedding night out with male friends
a male deer is a hart or buck

explanation.walkthrough: A stag party is the British name for a bachelor party.
explanation.definitionFit: Stag names both a male-only pre-wedding party and a male deer.

clue.text: See 7
Threat to little boy in mutual trouble

indicators.note: the boy sits within the jumbled letters, so in signals a container
letters in trouble are disturbed and rearranged

parts.note: Tim is a diminutive of Timothy, a boy's name

explanation.surface: A threat to a youngster caught in a shared dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' reads like a noun after 'mutual', but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: An ultimatum is a final demand backed by a threat of consequences.

clue.text: S kid counted fifty pegs wrongly

indicators.note: placed wrongly means the letters are put in a different order

explanation.surface: A child miscounts fifty clothes pegs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrongly' rearranges all nineteen letters of KID COUNTED FIFTY PEGS.
explanation.definitionFit: Sticky toffee pudding is a British dessert of date sponge in toffee sauce.

clue.text: S ingredient — inchoate depression

annotationWithheld.why: S ingredient — inchoate depression (9): COL in CHOATE, where 'inchoate' gives both the container indicator IN and the fodder CHOATE, one word doing two jobs

clue.text: Maybe seeing's beginning

indicators.note: maybe suggests the letters could form something else

parts.note: the letters of the word with its S, taken as written

explanation.surface: Perhaps seeing is where everything starts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' rearranges SEEINGS, including the S of the possessive. Genesis is also the Bible's first book.
explanation.definitionFit: Genesis means the origin or coming into being of something.

clue.text: S alcoholic drinks, heated, fatal to Goliath

parts.note: slings are sweetened spirit drinks such as the gin sling
heated means hot

explanation.surface: Sweet cocktails, warmed, prove deadly to the Philistine giant.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Bible David killed Goliath with a stone from his sling.
explanation.definitionFit: A slingshot is the stone-throwing weapon that felled the biblical giant.

clue.text: White range?

parts.note: people of European descent are called Caucasian, after these mountains

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: 'white' as in Caucasian, a name taken from the mountain chain.
explanation.definitionFit: The Caucasus is a mountain chain between the Black and Caspian Seas.

clue.text: Tress twice, first time with dropped letter forming obstruction

indicators.note: the first of the two words loses a letter, so a deletion

parts.note: both hair and lock mean a tress
both hair and lock mean a tress

explanation.surface: A lock of hair snagging and causing a blockage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tress twice' supplies two different synonyms; the dropped letter is the H that Cockney speech famously drops.
explanation.definitionFit: An airlock is a bubble of air blocking the flow in a pipe.

clue.text: Raptor on a string?

definitions.meaning: a toy flown in the wind on a line

explanation.definitionFit: Kite names both a bird of prey and a toy flown in the wind at the end of a line.

clue.text: Female part, said to be drunk and sick?

indicators.note: said signals that the words are spoken

parts.note: pissed is slang for drunk, ill means sick

explanation.surface: A rude remark about a woman's role while drunk and unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pissed ill', drunk and sick in British slang, sounds like the flower part.
explanation.definitionFit: The pistil is the female reproductive organ of a flower.

clue.text: See 14
S, as it may be, died, as it may be

indicators.note: as it may be suggests letters arranged another way

parts.note: S stands for a sweet throughout this puzzle
d is the abbreviation for died in genealogies

explanation.surface: A dessert and a death, each as the case may be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as it may be' is used twice: first it rearranges the letters of the puzzle's S word, and at the end it defines a way fruit for a sweet may be cooked.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit for a sweet is often stewed, simmered slowly in liquid.

clue.text: Relieved French nobleman getting about for daughter

indicators.note: the nobleman goes around the little word, so about signals a container

parts.note: a comte is a French count

explanation.surface: A French count is calmed by a visit from his daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting' is only a link; the count is the French title comte, not a nobleman's English rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Comforted means soothed, given relief from distress.

clue.text: Reversible note or dose

definitions.meaning: a half note in music whose letters read the same both ways
a tiny apothecaries' measure of liquid, a drop

explanation.definitionFit: A minim is both a half note in music and one sixtieth of a fluid dram.

clue.text: Vision could be jolly

definitions.meaning: both mean a lot, as in 'a ... better' or 'jolly good'

explanation.definitionFit: Sight is eyesight, and colloquially 'a sight' means very much, as jolly does.

clue.text: FT in group S, basically

indicators.note: one piece sits inside another, so in signals a container

parts.note: a set is a group
the Financial Times refers to itself in editorials as we

explanation.surface: The Financial Times in a set of letters, put simply.
explanation.walkthrough: A newspaper's editorial voice speaks as 'we'. S, at its base, is the word the puzzle uses it for.
explanation.definitionFit: S abbreviates sweet throughout this puzzle, so spelt out in full it is this word.

clue.text: S of the day, say

indicators.note: say signals the words are spoken

parts.note: the day of rest, the Sabbath

explanation.surface: A dessert described as the dish of the day.
explanation.definitionFit: A sundae is an ice-cream dessert with toppings, served in a tall glass.

clue.text: Unimportant affair at a fair

definitions.meaning: a minor diversion away from the main event
a small booth or show beside the main attraction

explanation.definitionFit: A sideshow is a fairground booth, and figuratively any minor distraction.

clue.text: Mathematician S with 21 down

definitions.meaning: one who sums, or adds up
a British dessert of bread lined with soft fruit, served chilled

explanation.definitionFit: A summer is literally one who adds figures, and summer pudding is a British fruit dessert.

clue.text: A fool and a 1950s boy are shaken

parts.note: a git is a foolish or contemptible person, British slang
a Ted, or Teddy boy, was a 1950s British youth in Edwardian dress

explanation.surface: A fool and a Teddy boy are rattled.
explanation.walkthrough: GIT is British slang for an idiot; Teds were 1950s youths in drape jackets.
explanation.definitionFit: Agitated means stirred up or disturbed, as something shaken is.
